title: 'Under the Skin' is kind of like the photo negative of 'Poor Things'

commenti.body: [removed]

I absolutely love Under the Skin. Never made the thematic connection with Poor Things. But I see exactly what you're saying about this connection.


I don't have much insight to add, because I think both films are relatively simple to analyze and you did that perfectly.


All I'll add is that protagonist doesn't have any moral qualifications to it, if that's why you're hesitant to use it for Under the Skin. It just means primary role, and ScarJo very much is.

I thought the same thing.

Poor Things has the satire ramped up to a higher degree, with Emma Stone's childmind being able to thoroughly dispatch all male oncomers. 

Poor Things also has more pronounced female characters offering glimpses to Emma Stone that the possibilities within her power far outstripe her current imaginings.

Under the Skin, character growth is emphasized in your great example, and differs from Poor Things in that Emma Stone seems to be growing towards something we can already conceive, while Scarlett Johansson's character seems to be beyond comprehension even as we see it's development

>the fact that it's also only men being killed in some ways feels like a twist on the conventions of the genre, which historically has a tendency to punish promiscuous women more than any other specific demographic.


I would say that while you might be right in general, the *femme fatale* is also a total archetype, and typically does exactly this thing, punish men for their sexualiy. Thinking further now that I said it, one might even frame the whole of Under the Skin as somehow a variation on that theme, maybe pushing it to a certain limit. 


I would specify that I am maybe thinking of a certain subset, the spyfilm/assassin variant. I think in general femme fatale also applies to e.g "crazy but hot" types that guys fall for and then it ruins them, but here I am thinking of coldblooded professional, the type you get in e.g. Bond or film noir movies.


Vibewise it just hits home, the femme fatale is similarily ice cold but sexy, she "devours" men, in her coldness she is alien, we struggle to imagine what she is thinking or feeling, as it is hard to imagine someone being so invulnerable yet superior in the sexual domain.


>In Under the Skin, this comes from the alien picking up a hitchhiker with a severe facial deformity, and realizing that this is the first form of real interaction he's experienced with another human in a very long time. After looking in the mirror, she lets the man go - the first discernable act of empathy from someone who very recently left an infant to die without a second thought. The first sign that a real act of change is taking place.



I think this is propably the generally correct emotional reading, also taking into account the metamorphosis imagery at the end, but I think its also crucial that the film really sticks to its "alien unknowability" to the end. We are meant to reach for the empathy explanation but then also doubt it at the same time, no further final point is made to really nail our interpretation down, it could have just as well been some weird alien logic. Same with all that happens in the third act. Yes there is obviously some kind of change from her icecold actions from before, she seems more human, but the point seems similarly obvious in the opposite direction, it is perhaps not that, we are meant to be kept in this tension, struggle with our natural anthropomorphizing instincts.


Its just this kind of Lynch stuff, I would think Glazer himself doesnt have a completely coherent take on it all that he is just not telling us, he really works on that impressionistic, alien level where the unknowability, even to himself is the point.

Great write-up! Totally true, I like that they didn't go for some kind of cheesy out of making her truly become human or something, the fact that it sheds the false identity at the end also confirms this; it's more like it was trying on empathy as a costume the way it was using ScarJo's skin - testing it to see what would happen, but not necessarily changed by it in an immutable way.

Very well said. My creative partner and I wrote [a huge literary deconstruction](https://filmcolossus.com/under-the-skin-explained/) of Under the Skin a couple years ago and it really helped me appreciate the nuance of the movie. A lot of which you summarized very nicely here. 

The Under the Skin story of discovering empathy and compassion is actually quite beautiful and profound. But then also confounded by a discover of humanity's capacity for darkness. So you get this inversion where the alien is initially a predator then is won over by people, only to discover that people can also be predators. 

What's crazy is that the novel doesn't end that way at all. She gets in a car crash and burns in the crash. It's a lot less interesting/compelling/meaningful. 

And then Poor Things, Bella does have an awakening of empathy for others, but the movie keeps her as so self-invested that I feel like it doesn't have the same impact. Granted, it's more accessible, so it probably actually reaches people in a way that Under the Skin may not. But it also feels a bit more about self-actualization than a broader appreciation for humanity. Don't get me wrong, part of Bella's self-actualization is tearing down class boundaries, which is why we get her, at the end, in a kind of utopia. You imagine what she's created at her home she'll try and engender elsewhere. So the idea is there. But it just seems so much more impactful to me in Under the Skin.

I, politely so, very much disagree with your last two paragraphs. Everything in the movie points toward her discovering empathy then practicing it. There's really nothing left to doubt. Scene by scene, the goal is to establish her initial coldness and then introduce more and more aspects that have her not only admire humans but desire to be like them, which culminates in her act of empathy. And then literally running away from her alien handler, a denial of her responsibility, so she can go try and have a human life, which she is sad to discover will not be possible. She can't eat the food, she can't have sex. 

I would argue that's absolutely nothing that suggests we're supposed to maintain that tension with our natural anthropomorphizing. That would be the case if, say, she did something cruel to the man who tried to help her. Or, if in the woods, we saw her harm someone for no reason. Then we'd have to wonder if we were mistaken about her turn to empathy. But there's legitimately nothing that signals anything in that direction. 

I would argue that Glazer 100% has a completely coherent take. This is what he said in an interview, alongside the screenwriter. 

---

**Jonathan:** The hardest part of the film was to chart her drift actually. It couldn’t be about one thing, we didn’t want this axiom where everything turned on this one moment and it was this epiphany.

**Walter:** We had to find steps where the transition would occur, both understood from the perspective of this monster, but then also understood from the perspective of a burgeoning consciousness where the sensibilities of empathy and of understanding were starting to attach themselves to this sentient being. A sentient being was operating without remorse, was totally ruthless, and had no hesitation in doing the most outrageous sort of things. But to see this consciousness creeping in was the balancing act.

**Jonathan:** It needed to be a glimmer on a Monday, a hunch on a Tuesday, a nascent idea on a Wednesday…We wanted to chart that drift towards her decision.

**Walter:** We were looking for something that felt cinematic and powerful, but we were also looking for the truth of that transition. And actually the pull between those two ambitions opened up a very beautiful space. The scene where she falls over is so simple and so human and that’s what I loved about it. I loved the idea of these people coming to help her. You just think, this extreme predator is in the midst of these things that she has no regard for but they’re prepared to lend a hand. There’s something in the vocabulary of that moment that just opens your mind up.

**Jonathan:** She’s pulled to her feet by human kindness, so something happens there, a jolt.

**Walter:** A lot of the conversations that we had were about the fact that she is encased in something that’s a very sophisticated protective shield. There’s a lot of attention paid to the way she’s moving and a sense of this thing moving through space and that sense that there’s a balancing act going on. She’s almost like this very sophisticated craft that should never fall over, and when she does, that tells you that something’s defective; something’s out of whack with the performance of the machine.

---

Someone who doesn't have a completely coherent take wouldn't be talking about charting the characters' draft. They would say something more vague, like "We just went with what felt natural in the moment and figured it out we filmed." This was a project that Glazer worked on for a decade? It was definitely a fully formed thing for him.

I think you were closer in your initial post. Don't be swayed by this. She wasn't trying on empathy as a costume. It was a legitimate thing she wanted. If it was merely something she was trying on, then, at the end, she would have reverted back to her previous femme fatale ways. Instead, she becomes the victim of a human predator. 

She doesn't shed the false identity, it's torn away from her by the guy who tries to prey on her. It's a tragic conclusion.

Alright, I respectfully admit to being totally owned. I wasnt so into the film to deeply research it or more properly decode it, and read some critics saying stuff along my lines, so I thought thats a valid take, but what you seems coherent and director says too, so seems we were all wrong. Would have to watch it again with that input to make more sense of it then.
Could you link that full interview if its available please, would be interested in reading it?

Here you are: https://medium.com/@Film4/beneath-the-surface-an-oral-history-of-under-the-skin-a62173045c0a

And a literary analysis of the film: https://filmcolossus.com/under-the-skin-explained/

Nothing to apologize for! Sorry if I came off intensely. I just get too passionate about this stuff lol. If we were in person, it would have been friendly earnest. But online, tone can read so critical.
Nono, all came across perfectly good! I was just wrong and you explained it very well. Will also take a look at your thesis later, very interested in it!

It's quite interesting to note that, with Poor Things being originally set in Glasgow, there was a tiny bit of controversy surrounding the movie adaptation when they decided to change the setting, choosing not to even film in Scotland. Under The Skin, of course, is filmed entirely in Scotland, with a large part taking place in Glasgow.
And *you're* Film *Colossus* and *not* Film *Hulk*?

I read an interview with Lanthimos where he said he wasn't comfortable setting the film in Scotland as he couldn't speak for the Scottish experience as a Greek director. Which made me laugh because taking on a story about the female experience as a male director is such an obviously more ambitious and controversial project.

> I absolutely love Under the Skin. Never made the thematic connection with Poor Things. 

They are both 'fish out of water' films where the protagonist is learning a new world and exploring stuff for the first time much like "My Fair Lady".

Interesting points. I think Garland’s Ex Machina fits into the conversation here as well. I found Poor Things had lots in common with Ex Machina, with Ramy Youssef’s performance dovetailing nicely with Domnhall Gleason’s character, and Mark Ruffalo similar in many ways to Oscar Isaac’s in their relationships with Bella/Ava

People may appreciate this analysis of the film and the book it is drawn from.

"Within Under the Skin, we experience a sort of dissonance between her sexualized body that we’re used to which asks: what is expected of that body, what’s done to that body, and what’s literally under the skin of that body within the film? It parallels the rarified space celebrities and attractive women occupy under the male gaze, one of titillation and then of fear. The Female exists within a structure, the same structure which has burned through several bodies just like hers. She starts as a terrifying cog in an alien machine who is unable to fill the role normally prescribed to women, so she is violently attacked. Under the Skin is an exploration of these themes we have been grappling with for a long time. Glazer’s film blends science-fiction, horror, and celebrity culture, with the ultimate question: what is identity and how changeable are our perceptions of it?"
